topics.title: Design a Parking Lot
topics.summary: The most frequently asked LLD problem: a multi-floor parking lot with typed slots, tickets, pluggable slot allocation and pricing, and thread-safe parking.
keyPoints: Typed slots and a VehicleType enum that lists allowed SlotTypes avoids scattered if/else.
SlotAllocationStrategy and PricingStrategy are Strategy pattern hooks for changing business rules.
ParkingService orchestrates; models stay simple; dependencies are injected via the constructor.
Tickets map ticketId to vehicle, slot and entry time; unpark removes the ticket and frees the slot.
Custom exceptions (ParkingFull, InvalidTicket) make failure paths explicit in the demo.
Thread safety: synchronized service methods for simplicity, or atomic per-slot occupy plus free-slot queues for scale.
Extensions like EV slots, display boards (Observer) and payment modes plug in without modifying core classes.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you make slot allocation O(1) instead of scanning all slots?
interviewQuestions.a: Maintain free slots in per-type data structures: for each `SlotType`, a `TreeSet` or `PriorityQueue` ordered by floor/distance from the gate (or a `ConcurrentLinkedDeque` if order does not matter). Parking polls the first free slot of the best allowed type; unparking adds the slot back. With a heap that is O(log n), with a queue O(1). This trades extra memory and bookkeeping for speed, and each structure must be updated atomically with the slot's state.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you handle two cars entering from different gates at the same time?
interviewQuestions.a: The race is in find-then-occupy. Options: (1) synchronize `park()` - simple but serialises all gates; (2) make `ParkingSlot.occupy()` an atomic compare-and-set that returns `false` if someone else took it, and retry allocation on failure; (3) keep concurrent free-slot queues where `poll()` atomically hands a slot to exactly one gate. Option 3 gives the best throughput. Ticket IDs come from an `AtomicLong` and active tickets live in a `ConcurrentHashMap`.

interviewQuestions.q: Why use the Strategy pattern for pricing?
interviewQuestions.a: Pricing rules change often and independently of parking logic: hourly, first-hour-free, weekend flat, peak surcharge, monthly passes. With `PricingStrategy`, `ParkingService` computes fees via an interface, and each rule is a separate, testable class. A new rule needs no change to existing code (OCP), and we can even pick a strategy at runtime based on day or customer. Rules can be combined using a decorator (e.g., `GstDecorator` wrapping any base strategy).

Conceptually there is one lot per deployment, so Singleton is a common answer, and if used it should be thread-safe (holder idiom or enum). However, static singletons are global state and hard to test or extend to multiple lots. I prefer creating one instance in `Main` (or via a DI container) and passing it to services. If the interviewer insists, I would implement the holder idiom and mention the testability trade-off.

topics.title: Design an Elevator System
topics.summary: Design a multi-elevator controller that dispatches hall requests using a pluggable scheduling strategy and moves cars with the SCAN (elevator) algorithm.
keyPoints: Separate hall calls (floor + direction, dispatched) from car calls (destination inside a specific elevator).
DispatchStrategy (Strategy pattern) picks the elevator; a cost function favours idle or on-the-way cars.
Each elevator keeps upStops and downStops TreeSets to implement the LOOK algorithm efficiently.
Simulate time with step() ticks so behaviour is deterministic and demoable in Main.
Elevator state (IDLE, MOVING, MAINTENANCE) controls behaviour; upgrade to full State pattern when doors and emergencies are added.
Validate floors and exclude maintenance cars in dispatch; synchronize per-elevator mutations.
Discuss FCFS vs SCAN vs LOOK trade-offs and peak-hour or zone strategies as extensions.

interviewQuestions.q: Which scheduling algorithm would you use for an elevator and why?
interviewQuestions.a: LOOK, a refinement of SCAN: the car keeps moving in its current direction serving all stops on the way and reverses only when there are no more requests ahead. FCFS causes excessive travel and unfair waits; Shortest-Seek-First can starve far floors. LOOK bounds waiting time and minimises direction changes. Implementation: two sorted sets per elevator (`upStops`, `downStops`); `ceiling()` and `floor()` give the next stop in O(log n).

interviewQuestions.q: How does the controller choose which elevator serves a hall call?
interviewQuestions.a: Through a pluggable `DispatchStrategy`. My default computes a cost per elevator: distance if idle; distance plus pending stops if the car is moving toward the floor in the requested direction; a large penalty if the car must first reverse. Elevators in maintenance or at full capacity are excluded. The minimum-cost car wins. Alternative strategies - least loaded, zone-based, or predictive for peak hours - can be swapped in without touching the controller.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you model door opening, closing and emergencies?
interviewQuestions.a: With the State pattern. States such as `Idle`, `MovingUp`, `MovingDown`, `DoorsOpen`, `Maintenance` and `Emergency` implement a common interface with `onTick()`, `onRequest()`, `openDoor()` and `closeDoor()`. Each state decides legal actions and the next state: for example, `MovingUp` ignores `openDoor()`, and `Emergency` rejects new requests and moves to the nearest floor. This removes nested `if (state == ...)` checks from the `Elevator` class.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you make this work concurrently with real time?
interviewQuestions.a: Each elevator runs its movement loop on a `ScheduledExecutorService` tick. Requests arrive from many threads, so `addStop` and `step` are synchronized per elevator (or use a lock), and the dispatcher reads elevator state under that lock or from a consistent snapshot. Requests can be submitted to a `BlockingQueue` that a dispatcher thread consumes, decoupling button presses from scheduling decisions.

topics.title: Design Splitwise (Expense Sharing)
topics.summary: A favourite Flipkart/PhonePe machine-coding problem: track shared expenses with equal, exact and percentage splits, maintain balances and simplify debts.
keyPoints: Store money as long paise to avoid floating-point errors; format only for display.
SplitStrategy (EQUAL, EXACT, PERCENT) plus a factory keyed by SplitType keeps split logic extensible.
Each strategy validates its own input: exact amounts must sum to total, percents to 100.
Handle rounding deterministically: one participant absorbs the remainder.
BalanceSheet as Map<user, Map<user, amount>> updates both directions symmetrically in O(1) per participant.
Debt simplification uses net balances and greedy matching of largest creditor and debtor.
Groups, passbook, settle-up and concurrency are the standard follow-ups.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you simplify debts in Splitwise?
interviewQuestions.a: Compute each user's **net balance** (total owed to them minus total they owe). Users with positive net are creditors, negative are debtors. Repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor (two heaps), transfer `min(credit, -debt)`, and push back any remainder. This needs at most n-1 transactions and runs in O(n log n). Finding the absolute minimum number of transactions is NP-hard, so the greedy approach is the standard practical answer.

interviewQuestions.q: Why should you not use double for money?
interviewQuestions.a: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, and errors accumulate across many expenses, causing balances that do not net to zero. Use integer minor units (`long` paise) or `BigDecimal` with an explicit `RoundingMode`. In machine coding, `long` paise is simpler and faster; convert to rupees only for display.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you handle 100 split equally among 3 people?
interviewQuestions.a: Integer division gives 3333 paise each with 1 paise remainder. Assign the remainder deterministically, typically to the first participant (or the payer), giving 33.34, 33.33, 33.33. The key requirement is that the splits always sum exactly to the total, so balances stay consistent. The same idea applies to percent splits: compute all but the last participant by rounding and give the last one `total - allocated`.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you add a new split type like SHARE (ratio-based)?
interviewQuestions.a: Create `ShareSplit implements SplitStrategy` that takes share counts, computes `total * share / sumShares` for each participant with remainder handling, and validates that shares are positive. Register it in the factory under `SplitType.SHARE` and extend the parser. No changes to `BalanceSheet`, `Expense` or other strategies are needed - that is the Open/Closed benefit of the Strategy pattern.

topics.title: Design BookMyShow (Movie Ticket Booking)
topics.summary: Design a movie ticket booking system with cities, theatres, shows and seats, focusing on preventing double booking with seat locks and timeouts.
keyPoints: Model City/Theatre/Screen/Seat/Movie/Show/Booking; a Show binds a movie to a screen at a time.
Book in two phases: lock seats (PENDING) then confirm on payment success or release on failure/timeout.
Seat locking must be all-or-nothing across multiple seats to avoid partial bookings.
Locks carry an expiry so abandoned checkouts free seats automatically.
SeatLockProvider interface lets in-memory locks be swapped for Redis or DB constraints in production.
Pricing per seat category is a Strategy; booking status transitions model the lifecycle.
Production safety nets: DB unique constraint on (show, seat), optimistic locking, idempotent payments.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you prevent double booking of the same seat?
interviewQuestions.a: Two layers. First, a temporary **seat lock** taken atomically for all requested seats when the user proceeds to pay: in-memory with a synchronized check-then-lock per show, or in Redis with `SET seatKey user NX PX 300000`. Second, a **final guarantee** at confirmation: a database unique constraint on `(show_id, seat_id)` in the booked-seats table, or optimistic locking with a version column, so even if locks fail only one insert succeeds. Losers get a clear "seat unavailable" error.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do seat locks need a timeout?
interviewQuestions.a: Users abandon payment, close the app or lose connectivity. Without expiry, those seats stay locked forever and the show looks sold out. A TTL (typically 5-10 minutes) automatically frees them. Expiry is checked lazily on every availability query and actively by a scheduled cleanup job that also moves the related bookings from `PENDING` to `EXPIRED`. If payment succeeds after expiry, the system must re-verify seat availability or refund.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you scale this to millions of users on a blockbuster release?
interviewQuestions.a: Cache show listings and seat maps (read-heavy) with short TTLs or event-based invalidation. Shard booking data by show id so locks for a show live on one partition. Use Redis for seat locks for low latency, and a queue/virtual waiting room to throttle traffic spikes. Keep payment asynchronous with idempotency keys and confirm via webhooks. The DB unique constraint stays as the correctness backstop.

interviewQuestions.q: Which design patterns did you use and why?
interviewQuestions.a: Strategy for `SeatLockProvider` (in-memory vs distributed) and `PricingStrategy` (category, weekend or dynamic pricing). A State-like lifecycle for `Booking` (`PENDING -> CONFIRMED / CANCELLED / EXPIRED`) with guarded transitions. Facade: `BookingService` hides locking, pricing and persistence behind `createBooking` and `confirm`. Observer as an extension for notifications and waitlists. Each pattern isolates something likely to change.
